title: TC2-01781
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): She appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), rendered on January 4, 2022, denying her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Kenya. She appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), rendered on January 4, 2022, denying her claim for refugee protection. The Appellant requests that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD or that the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination.1

The following is a brief summary of the Appellant's allegations contained in her Basis of Claim (BOC) form narrative. The Appellant is a 29-year-old woman from Nakuru who alleges that she is bisexual. She alleges that she had a long-term relationship with a woman who I will refer to as "J" in Kenya. In 2018, the Appellant had a child with a man with whom she had a brief relationship or encounter. The child remains in Kenya with the Appellant's mother.

In 2020, the Appellant and J were caught kissing in the restroom at a bar. People in the bar came to see what was happening, including the Appellant's cousin, XXXX, who was also at the bar that night. This led to the Appellant's community becoming aware of the Appellant's sexual orientation. The Appellant began to receive phone threats from a man who identified himself as a member of the Mungiki, an outlawed gang or group in Kenya. He threatened to kill the Appellant and her family. The Appellant sought refuge with her brother XXXX in Nairobi, but her brother began receiving threatening phone calls from people who identified themselves as Mungiki.
The Appellant applied for a Canadian student visa, which was issued in XXXX 2020. She left Kenya on January 13, 2021 for Canada, where she made her claim for refugee protection.

The RPD rejected the Appellant's claim on the basis of credibility. The RPD found that the Appellant provided inconsistent evidence about material aspects of her claim, which was not reasonably explained, and the remaining evidence did not overcome the credibility concerns identified. As a result, the RPD found that the Appellant had not established, on a balance of probabilities, that she is bisexual. The Appellant advances several arguments on appeal, which I discuss in detail in my assessment below.

I dismiss the appeal pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).2 The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention3 refugee nor a person in need of protection. After considering all of the evidence, I find that the Appellant has not credibly established that she is bisexual or that she was ever in a same-sex relationship, that she was threatened in Kenya on that basis, or that she is perceived to be bisexual in Kenya. Accordingly, I find that the Appellant has not established that she faces a serious possibility of persecution under section 96 of the IRPA, or a risk as defined in section 97 of the IRPA, in Kenya.

According to the law,4 I can only accept evidence that: (a) arose after the RPD decision; or (b) was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or (c) that the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, according to the decisions in Singh and Raza, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.5

The Appellant submitted a personal affidavit and a letter from her alleged current same-sex partner, "A," in Canada, accompanied by a copy of A's identity card. The Appellant's affidavit explains that she and A have been together for more than a year but they "became closer" and began a relationship in XXXX of last year (2021). A's letter indicates that she ended her relationship with her previous partner in XXXX 2021 and began a relationship with the Appellant that same month.

The RPD decision was rendered on January 4, 2022. Both the affidavit and the letter from A post-date the RPD decision. However, they both indicate that the relationship between them began in XXXX 2021. Counsel indicates in the Memorandum that "the letter could not be expected to have been provided earlier because the Appellant's same-sex relationship was at a very incipient stage when the RPD was deliberating and deciding the claim"6 and "the partner was not likely to be persuaded to issue such a letter during the very first days of the relationship."7

I do not find that these documents meet the criteria in section 110(4) of the IRPA. Although the documents post-date the RPD decision, the content of the documents must also be examined. In this case, the relationship between the Appellant and A is alleged to have begun before the RPD decision. While Counsel argues that, at the time of the RPD decision, it was early in the relationship for the Appellant to ask A for such a letter, this does not explain why the Appellant could not have otherwise submitted evidence of her relationship with A before the RPD. Specifically, this does not explain why the Appellant could not have submitted her personal affidavit indicating that she was in a relationship with A, even if the letter from A did not accompany her affidavit, given that she had entered into the relationship with A before the RPD's decision.

More importantly, the Appellant herself has not explained why she did not obtain a letter from A before the RPD decision. While it is Counsel's submission that this is because it was a new relationship, this is Counsel's submission; it is not evidence. The Appellant did not indicate in her affidavit that she tried but was unable to obtain such a letter before the RPD decision. She indicated that her partner "was persuaded to issue the support letter only now that our relationship is more consolidated." However, this is vague and there is no indication as to whether the Appellant tried to "persuade" her partner to provide such a letter earlier (specifically, before the RPD decision, which is the relevant timeline for the consideration of new evidence under section 110(4) of the IRPA), or when it was that their relationship became more "consolidated." Considering the foregoing, I find that the Appellant has not demonstrated that the personal affidavit and letter from A were not reasonably available at the time of the RPD decision or that the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected to bring this evidence before the RPD. Section 110(4) of the IRPA is not a permissive provision. I am unable to accept evidence that does not meet its criteria. Accordingly, the new evidence submitted by the Appellant is rejected.

The Appellant requested an oral hearing.8 However, according to section 110(6) of the IRPA, I am only able to hold an oral hearing if new evidence has been admitted. As no new evidence has been accepted in this case, I am unable to hold a hearing.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.9

In considering this appeal, I have taken into account and applied Chairperson's Guideline 9: Proceedings Before the IRB involving Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Expression and Sex Characteristics10 (SOGIESC Guideline). While the guiding principles contained in the SOGIESC Guideline are not mandatory, decision-makers are expected to apply them or provide a reasoned justification for not doing so.11 Credibility

I have conducted an independent assessment of all the evidence, including the Appellant's Record in its entirety and the oral testimony. For the following reasons, I find that the RPD's conclusion was correct. Inconsistencies in Appellant's evidence about material aspects of Appellant's claim Timeline of relationship with J

The RPD found that the Appellant offered inconsistent evidence about the only same-sex relationship she alleged to have had in Kenya (her relationship with J), in that there were discrepancies between her BOC narrative and testimony about the timeline of their relationship, including when they broke up and when they reconnected, and when they each had other relationships or encounters with men.12

The Appellant does not specifically contest this finding on appeal. In the Memorandum, Counsel argues, more generally, that the psychotherapist's report in evidence offers insight into the irregularities in the Appellant's evidence.13 I consider the psychotherapist's report separately below. Upon independent assessment, I agree with and adopt the findings of the RPD in this regard, and I agree with the RPD for the same reasons as articulated by the RPD that the Appellant did not reasonably explain these irregularities in the evidence.

The Appellant's allegation about her relationship with J is central to her claim, in that it was alleged to be her only same-sex relationship in Kenya, and it was her relationship with J that is alleged to ultimately have led to the discovery of her sexual orientation. The RPD asked on several occasions for an explanation for the discrepancies in the Appellant's evidence about her relationship with J. First, the Appellant was evasive and did not explain the discrepancies,14 and later the Appellant offered a convoluted explanation in which her testimony evolved and she explained that their relationship did not in fact continue after 2017 and they decided to take a break, and then in 2019 they reconnected15 and rekindled their relationship.16 I am not satisfied either with the Appellant's explanations, as they do not ultimately address the inconsistencies or offer any substantive explanation.

Considering this, I find that these are material discrepancies that significantly undermine the Appellant's allegation of having been in a same-sex relationship in Kenya. Given that this is the only relationship she alleges to have been in in Kenya, and the discovery of her relationship with J is alleged to have been the catalyst for her departure from Kenya, I find that this significantly undermines the Appellant's credibility generally. Threats

I also agree with the RPD that the Appellant's testimony about the threats that are alleged to have led her to flee Kenya was vague and lacking in detail.17 The Appellant does not specifically contest this finding either, except as I have indicated above with respect to the psychological evidence, and I agree with and adopt the reasoning of the RPD in this regard. Despite being asked numerous questions about the threats, the Appellant's testimony was consistently vague, for instance, as to when the threats began, what was said, how the Appellant responded to the threats, whether J also received any threats.18

As the threats from the Mungiki are central to her claim, and she alleges that she began receiving them as a result of having been caught kissing J, and is the reason she alleges that she left Kenya, she can be expected to provide adequately detailed testimony in this regard. I find that her inability to do so undermines her credibility about what led her to leave Kenya. The RPD's finding was correct. I do not find that the Appellant's psychological condition explains this either, for the reasons articulated in more detail below. Who knew about the Appellant's sexual orientation

The RPD also found that the Appellant provided internally inconsistent testimony about who, in Kenya, was aware of her sexual orientation.19 The Appellant does not specifically contest this finding in the Memorandum, except that, as I have mentioned, the Appellant indicates that the psychotherapist's report offers insight into her testimony generally.20 Again, I have addressed this specifically below.

I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's evidence contains a material discrepancy in this regard. The RPD asked the Appellant a clear question at the beginning of the hearing about who in Kenya is aware of her sexual orientation. The Appellant answered that only her mother, father, brothers and cousin know.21 The RPD asked the Appellant if anyone else knew, to which she answered in the negative.22 The Appellant later indicated that the community became aware because she was caught kissing J, and the Mungiki began to threaten her. She was specific in her testimony that "so many people knew about my sexuality."23 This, she explained, was perhaps how the Mungiki got her phone number, because she indicated her phone number on her social media and they could have gotten it that way because so many people knew about her sexual orientation.24

The RPD Member asked the Appellant to explain this internal discrepancy, namely, why she testified earlier that it was only her mother, father, brothers and cousin who knew. The Appellant's explanation was evasive. She indicated that her family members knew but the other group came to know later on.25 I do not find that the Appellant ultimately provided a substantive explanation for the discrepancy. Accordingly, I draw a further negative credibility inference. The RPD's finding in this regard was correct. Efforts to seek protection

The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence about her efforts to seek protection in Kenya was internally inconsistent, and that she omitted from her BOC any mention of having sought protection in Kenya.26 The Appellant testified that she did not try to seek the help of the police from the Mungiki.27 The Appellant nonetheless submitted a letter from the Ministry of Interior and Coordination of National Government, written by XXXX XXXX in her area of Nakuru.28 The letter indicates that the Appellant reported the death threats from the Mungiki in XXXX 2020. However, the Appellant's evidence is that she and J were not caught together until XXXX 2020.

The RPD asked the Appellant to explain how it could be that the letter indicated that she reported the death threats in XXXX 2020.29 The Appellant explained that she did not go to the police but she talked to XXXX XXXX who is in charge of her traditional community.30 She further explained that there might have been a miscommunication or a mistake on her part, and she may have indicated the wrong date to her mother (who requested the letter) when explaining to her what happened.31 The RPD found that this further undermines the Appellant's allegation about being caught with J and threatened by the Mungiki.32

The Appellant does not specifically contest this finding in the Memorandum. Upon independent assessment, I agree with the RPD's findings as to the discrepancies identified, and I am not satisfied with the Appellant's explanation. The Appellant has submitted the letter from XXXX XXXX in support of her claim. She is expected to know the contents of her documentary evidence. If there was a mistake in XXXX XXXX letter, it is expected that she would seek to have it corrected or, if that was not possible, to bring the error to the attention of the Board before being confronted on it in her refugee hearing. Further still, if the Appellant requested the help of XXXX XXXX, it is unclear why she did so, considering her evidence that she could not report the Mungiki to the authorities because she felt she would risk arrest for her same-sex activities. Considering the foregoing, I find that these discrepancies further undermine the Appellant's credibility. Psychotherapist's report

The Appellant's documentary evidence also conflicts with the Appellant's other evidence in certain respects, notably the psychotherapist's report. The Appellant indicated that she told the psychotherapist about her experiences in Kenya.33 The RPD noted that the psychotherapist's report contained inconsistencies about the details of the events alleged to have been experienced by the Appellant in Kenya, including discrepancies as to where the Appellant and J were caught kissing, when the Appellant and her male partner broke up, when the Appellant and J reconciled, and when threats by the Mungiki began.34

The RPD confronted the Appellant on these various inconsistencies.35 The Appellant explained, with respect to the discrepancy about where she and J were caught kissing, that the psychotherapist must have misunderstood her.36 The RPD confronted the Appellant on the other inconsistencies, and the Appellant's explanations were evasive and did not ultimately explain the discrepancies.37

I agree with the RPD that the Appellant has not adequately explained the discrepancies and I also agree with the RPD that this further undermines her credibility. Counsel argues, on the basis of the Court's decisions in Mico38 and Gurses39 that the purpose of the psychotherapist's report was not to prove persecution in Kenya but to alert the RPD to the Appellant's current mental condition.40 I cannot agree with this argument, in the circumstances of this case. The Appellant has submitted the psychotherapist's report in support of her claim. The Appellant is expected to know the contents of the evidence she has submitted in support of her claim. As such, even though the purpose of the psychotherapist's report is to provide insight into the psychological condition of the Appellant, if she knew the psychotherapist's report to contain information that conflicts with her own understanding of events, she could be expected to have sought to have this corrected or to have brought the errors to the Board's attention before being confronted on them in the RPD hearing. Accordingly, I find that the inconsistencies between the psychotherapist's report and the Appellant's other evidence, and her submission of the psychotherapist's report notwithstanding these inconsistencies, further undermine her credibility.

The ability of the psychotherapist's report to explain the deficiencies in the Appellant's testimony is a separate issue altogether, which I assess below. Deficiencies in evidence not explained by psychological evidence and Consideration of Guidelines

The Appellant argues that the RPD "erred in assessing the Appellant's credibility in view of Chairperson (sic.) Guidelines 8 and 9 and Psychotherapy Report's findings."41 In this regard, Counsel describes Kenya as an "extremely homophobic society... where an individual must internalize their feelings, which was the Appellant's case for years."42

Counsel submits that the RPD did not explain how it implemented Guideline 8, which, she argues, provides for procedural accommodations which can be raised on the Member's own initiative.43 I am not persuaded by this argument. Counsel's argument is vague and it is not substantiated by an argument or explanation from Counsel as to how she submits that the Appellant should have been accommodated. Moreover, the Appellant was represented by counsel before the RPD, and there is no indication that any request was made for accommodation, nor was any request made for the designation of the Appellant as a vulnerable person. Nor did Counsel make any request for accommodation before the RAD, even though Counsel specifically points in the Memorandum to the psychotherapist's report in evidence and its note that the Appellant appears to her to be "a vulnerable person in need of help."44 If Counsel was of the view that the Appellant was in need of some form of accommodation, it was open to her (or to the Appellant's previous counsel) to identify the specific form of accommodation she submits the Appellant would benefit from and to request that at any point during her representation of the Appellant.

What is more, upon independent assessment, I disagree that the evidence supports that the RPD erred by not making a vulnerable person designation or offering other accommodation in the Appellant's case. I have listened carefully to the audio recording of the hearing, and I have considered, for instance, whether the Appellant could appreciate the nature of the proceeding. There is nothing "obvious"45 in the record that leads me to conclude that she could not do so or that she was unable to testify. While the hearing can be a stressful experience for any claimant, I note that the RPD Member maintained a calm atmosphere in the hearing room and took breaks periodically, and that her pace, tone and explanation of questions and concepts were appropriate to the Appellant's profile.

Counsel also reproduces certain sections of the SOGIESC Guideline and argues that the "internalization or repression of feelings over an extended period becomes a way of life which leaves its permanent mark on an individual's mental health. Often it becomes really difficult for an individual to be forthcoming and open, especially to a person in a position of authority."46 I cannot agree with this argument either, in the circumstances. While Counsel sets out certain sections of the SOGIESC Guideline, Counsel does not relate those specifically to the Appellant's case or specify if or in what way she submits the RPD did not follow the SOGIESC Guideline, beyond indicating that it can be difficult for people in the Appellant's circumstances to be forthcoming and open. This is also vague. It is insufficient to point to the Guideline without indicating how Counsel submits the RPD failed to follow it. Moreover, Counsel's assessment of the effects of the Appellant's alleged past experiences on her mental health or her ability to be forthcoming are her submissions; they are not evidence.

Regardless, I have conducted my own, independent assessment. In so doing, I have considered the report in evidence from psychotherapist XXXX XXXX, reporting on an assessment of the Appellant undertaken on XXXX XXXX, 2021.47 The RPD found that the psychotherapist's report indicates that the Appellant "may" have trouble with memory and that it does not adequately explain the Appellant's inability to recall important details of the events that led her to leave Kenya.48

Upon independent assessment, I cannot agree with Counsel's argument that the psychotherapist's report "offers invaluable insight as to why the Appellant's testimony appeared inconsistent and incoherent."49 Nor do I agree with Counsel's argument that the RPD's findings in paragraphs 18-19 of its decision "support a finding that, rather than the narrative being concocted, the likely cause for the defective testimony was the Appellant's mental health condition."50 Counsel has not explained why she submits these paragraphs of the RPD decision point to such a conclusion, and I do not find this to be the case. Moreover, it is the Appellant's burden to establish if any mental health or other conditions affected her ability to provide testimony; it is not the role of the decision-maker to speculate as to whether this is the case.

Upon independent assessment, I note that the psychotherapist indicates that the Appellant was referred to her by a doctor, who indicated that the Appellant had been diagnosed with symptoms of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX), XXXX and XXXX.51 The psychotherapist's report notes that the Appellant did not show any indications of abnormalities in her thought process and her thought content was clear and organized.52 The therapist reported her mood as being apprehensive and anxious, but she was able to remain focused and responded in a rational manner to all questions.53 The report discusses the Appellant's low mood and sleep problems, her worry about being returned to Kenya, and guilt at having left her daughter in Kenya. The report indicates that the Appellant's levels of XXXX and XXXX are both "severe," and that she is in the "moderate" range for XXXX XXXX.54

In addition, while I note that the psychotherapist refers to the Appellant's sexual orientation as the basis for her fear and refers to her description of the events he alleges to have experienced in Kenya, the Court has been clear that, with respect to the assessment of a psychological professional's evidence and the question of the assessment of credibility, "that opinion evidence is only as valid as the truth of the facts on which it is based."55 As such, while I accept that the Appellant exhibited or is exhibiting the symptoms described by the psychotherapist, I do not find that the therapist's report is probative in establishing the facts alleged, i.e. her sexual orientation or the incidents she alleges to have experienced in Kenya. With the foregoing in mind, I have considered the psychotherapist's report in so far as it may explain any irregularities in the Appellant's evidence.

Importantly, while the psychotherapist's report lists several symptoms, it does not indicate that the Appellant suffers from any appreciable memory or cognitive problems. The report indicates that, in respect of her XXXX symptoms, she may be subject to avoidance of memories and inability to recall parts of the event, especially when and if exposed to high stress and other triggering objects or events.56 Even if these could potentially arise when stressed, in the absence of any indication that the Appellant suffered from any cognitive or memory issues at the time of the hearing, I would be speculating if I was to conclude that any of those issues arose or affected her ability to testify at the RPD hearing. Further still, it is unclear which of the difficulties in the Appellant's testimony Counsel submits can be explained by the psychotherapist's report, and the Court has been clear that a psychiatric or psychologist's report submitted as evidence "cannot possibly serve as a cure-all for any and all deficiencies in a claimant's testimony."57

The Court has also been clear that where problems with testimony (e.g., inconsistencies, omissions) are found to be unrelated to the person's condition, expert evidence regarding that condition may be given little or no weight.58 In Zararsiz, the Court found the psychological report shed no light on the discrepancies in the testimony.59 In that case, an expert opined that the applicant met the diagnostic criteria for XXXX.60 The Court found that the RAD reasonably found that the expert report did not explain the deficiencies in the applicant's evidence, which arose not from his inability to recall details, but from significant inconsistencies between his statements at the port of entry and various iterations of his BOC narrative.

Considering the foregoing, while I accept that the Appellant suffered trauma in her life, I do not find that the psychotherapist's report serves to explain the significant and pervasive difficulties in the Appellant's testimony and evidence, including with respect to the core issue of her sexual orientation.

In my independent assessment, I have considered not only the psychotherapist's report but the whole of the evidence as to the Appellant's profile and circumstances. I note that the Appellant is an adult with an elevated level of education and work experience. She has completed a Bachelor's degree and almost completed a Master's degree.

Per the SOGIESC Guideline, I have considered whether there are cultural barriers that may explain the deficiencies in the Appellant's testimony.61 In this regard, I have also carefully reviewed the objective documentary evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP) on file concerning the treatment of LGBTIQ+ individuals in Kenya. This evidence indicates that same-sex relations are criminalized in Kenya, homophobic sentiments are pervasive and homosexuality is not widely socially accepted.62 I have considered this cultural backdrop and the possible influence of self-censorship on the Appellant's testimony. However, considering the extent of the inconsistencies and irregularities in her testimony, and how pervasive this was throughout her testimony, and also considering her particular profile, I do not find that the Appellant's cultural background adequately explains her inability to testify consistently about so many material aspects of her claim for refugee protection. The Appellant's remaining evidence does not overcome the credibility concerns
The Appellant submitted several documents in support of her claim, including the letter from XXXX XXXX, and four supporting affidavits. Letter from XXXX

The RPD found that, for the reasons explained above, XXXX XXXX letter contained inconsistencies vis-à-vis the Appellant's other evidence, which were not reasonably explained.63 The RPD also found that the letter does not make reference to the Appellant's sexual orientation. The RPD therefore found that the letter does not serve to corroborate the Appellant's allegations.64 I agree with and adopt the reasoning of the RPD in this regard, and I give the letter minimal weight in establishing the Appellant's allegations. Four supporting affidavits

The RPD found that the four supporting affidavits, from the Appellant's family members and from the visa agent who assisted the Appellant in obtaining her Canadian visa, were insufficient to outweigh the credibility concerns identified. I have assessed these affidavits independently.65 The affidavits refer to the Appellant's sexual orientation and her need to leave Kenya as a result. While I find no reason to conclude that these affidavits are not genuine, I do not find that they, together with the Appellant's other evidence, are sufficient to overcome the significant credibility concerns identified.

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by "rejecting" the four affidavits because they do not overcome the credibility issues.66 The Appellant also argues that the RPD "ignored" the affidavits.67 Upon independent assessment, I do not find that this accurately represents the RPD's findings. It is unclear how, as the Appellant submits, the RPD at once ignored and rejected this evidence. Moreover, I find that the RPD neither ignored nor rejected these documents, but explicitly found that they were insufficient in their weight to overcome the credibility concerns identified. I find no error in its reasoning in that regard.

The Appellant also argues that the RPD acknowledged that the Appellant provided some level of detail in her testimony,68 but that the RPD ignored the testimony in arriving at its adverse conclusion on credibility.69 However, I do not find this to be the case. The decision-maker is presumed to have considered all of the evidence and need not mention all of it in its decision. There is no indication that the RPD ignored the Appellant's testimony, and it was open to the RPD to assess whether the credible aspects of the Appellant's evidence, including her testimony, was sufficient to overcome the adverse credibility inferences drawn.

In my independent assessment, I have considered all of the Appellant's testimony. While there were problems with her testimony, as I have identified, the Appellant was able to provide some consistent testimony about her alleged discovery of her sexual orientation and her first experiences in actualizing her attraction to women. However, I do not find that this, in conjunction with any of her other evidence, is sufficient to overcome the credibility concerns identified. The RPD's finding in this regard was correct. The Appellant has not established a "sur place" claim

Counsel argues that the Appellant has established a "sur place" claim concerning the "continued risk the Appellant would face in Kenya... if she freely expresses her sexual identity and orientation like she does in Canada."70

I am not persuaded by this argument. I do not find that the Appellant has established, on a balance of probabilities, that she is in a same-sex relationship in Canada. I have not accepted the Appellant's new evidence in this regard, for the reasons already expressed above, and find that I have insufficient evidence before me to establish this allegation. I do not find that there is any other reason to find that the Appellant has established a "sur place" claim in Canada. It is not, for instance, the Appellant's evidence that she became bisexual in Canada or discovered her bisexual identity while in Canada, or that her actions in Canada otherwise expose her to risk in Kenya. Accordingly, the Appellant has not established a "sur place" claim. Conclusion regarding Appellant's credibility

Considering the foregoing, I find that the Appellant has not established her allegations on a balance of probabilities, including that she is bisexual, that her sexual orientation led her to leave Kenya, that she was or is being pursued by the Mungiki, that anyone in Kenya perceives her to be bisexual, or that she was or is in the same-sex relationship in Canada. Accordingly, I find that the Appellant has not established that she faces a serious possibility of persecution under section 96 of the IRPA because of her actual or perceived sexual orientation, or a risk as defined in section 97 of the IRPA in Kenya.

In addition, while Counsel makes submissions on state protection, I have not addressed them here because it is not necessary that I do so, given that I find the issue of the Appellant's credibility to be determinative in this case.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
